Researchers have increasingly turned their attention toward Technology-Enhanced Collaborative Writing (TECW) as a valuable tool for second language acquisition. Despite the rapid adoption of technology in education, there exists a notable research gap concerning the challenges and strategies encountered by Malaysian ESL (English as a Second Language) teachers when incorporating technology into their collaborative writing classrooms. This paper seeks to bridge this gap by shedding light on the specific challenges faced by ESL teachers in Malaysia and the strategies they employ to integrate technology effectively into collaborative writing instruction. The research employs the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT 2) Model to measure these challenges, employing qualitative data collection methods through interviews with four ESL teachers situated in Kuala Lumpur's Keramat District, all of whom are participants in the Bring-Your-Own-Device (BYOD) pilot program. These findings emphasize the strategies needed for ESL teachers to elevate the quality of their instruction aspects. Ultimately, this research hopes to provide valuable insights to guide teachers in crafting context-specific guidelines for TECW procedures and offers a foundational framework for enhancing ESL instruction in the Malaysian context. 1 Introduction There is no doubt that English is a compulsory subject in Malaysian students' educational programs, which spans their primary and secondary school years and lasts eleven years. In Malaysian schools, the English language curriculum emphasizes the development of four basic language skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing. These fundamental abilities are carefully taught to young students so they can become fluent English speakers. Despite years of study and committed attempts to acquire English, many students continue to have difficulties in obtaining higher levels of proficiency [1]. This raises awareness of the issue with English language education and learning. Teachers play an important role in engaging with students and scaffolding their learning process to assist them in enhancing their English language skills in the classroom [2]. These features distinguish collaborative writing from cooperative writing. Framing collaborative academic writing (CAW) as a pedagogical process, this systematic literature review explores how digital technologies and instructional strategies have been utilised to support students' engagement across the writing phases. A total of 27 peer-reviewed empirical studies, published between 2014 and 2024 and indexed in the Scopus database, were analysed using the PRISMA 2020 framework to ensure methodological rigour and transparency. The findings identified twenty types of technologies applied across the three phases of CAW including prewriting, in-writing, and post-writing. These technologies were categorised into five groups: collaborative study tools, classroom-based technologies, cloud-based word processors and shared documents, network-based social computing, and supporting tools. Frequently utilised platforms, including Google Docs, Moodle, Zoom, and WhatsApp, functioned either as interactive collaborative spaces that foster communication and idea co-construction or as task-supporting tools that facilitate drafting, feedback, and revision activities.In parallel, six core instructional strategies were identified: prewriting activities, scaffolding, peer review and feedback, collaborative revising and editing, reflective tasks, and collaborative note-taking. These strategies were systematically mapped across the writing phases, supporting not only the technical aspects of writing but also promoting collaborative interaction, critical thinking, and reflective learning practices. Importantly, the review highlights that successful TECAW implementation requires the intentional orchestration of technologies and instructional designs to align with the pedagogical goals at each stage of collaborative writing. The review emphasises that the effective integration of technology in CAW must be intentionally aligned with the pedagogical objectives at each stage of writing, ensuring that tools not only enhance task performance but also strengthen students' collaborative engagement and academic writing development. Overall, this study offers valuable insights for educators and researchers seeking to design student-centred, technology-supported writing instruction that reflects evolving digital pedagogies in higher education. Classification of teacher practices for technology-enhanced collaborative writing is organized around the phases of writing and the roles teachers play in supporting student collaboration. The evidence points to two main dimensions: **pedagogical phases** and **instructional strategies**. The Malaysian ESL TECW study frames collaborative writing as a non-linear, interactive process and emphasizes the need to scaffold students’ learning and align instruction with writing pedagogy [N1-F1]. The higher-education systematic review explicitly categorizes technologies across three writing phases—**prewriting, in-writing, and post-writing**—and maps six core instructional strategies across those phases [N3-F2]. These strategies include prewriting activities, scaffolding, peer review and feedback, collaborative revising and editing, reflective tasks, and collaborative note-taking [N3-F2].

The practices most commonly associated with technology use are those that require **shared authorship, structured pedagogical support, and task orchestration**. The review notes that frequently used platforms such as Google Docs, Moodle, Zoom, and WhatsApp function either as interactive collaborative spaces or as task-supporting tools for drafting, feedback, and revision [N3-F2]. This suggests that technology is especially salient for **collaborative idea construction, communication, and revision support**. The Malaysian study also emphasizes that teachers need strategies to elevate instruction aspects and guide context-specific guidelines for TECW procedures [N1-F1], reinforcing that technology is not merely a tool but a means to shape pedagogy.

Classification differs across studies and contexts because the framing varies by educational level and the nature of the writing task. The Malaysian study is centered on **ESL classrooms** and uses the UTAUT 2 model to examine challenges and strategies, focusing on implementation from cognitive, metacognitive, behavioural, and motivational aspects [N1-R2]. The higher-education systematic review, by contrast, is broader and methodologically more formal, analyzing empirical studies across 27 peer-reviewed sources and emphasizing intentional orchestration of technologies and instructional designs aligned with pedagogical goals [N3-F2]. It also explicitly categorizes technologies into five groups: collaborative study tools, classroom-based technologies, cloud-based word processors and shared documents, network-based social computing, and supporting tools [N3-F2]. The clearest classification is by **writing phase**. Before students begin writing, teachers support **orientation, scaffolding, task design, and initial collaboration setup**. Classification of teacher practices for technology-enhanced collaborative writing is organized around the phases of writing and the roles teachers play in supporting student collaboration. The evidence points to two main dimensions: **pedagogical phases** and **instructional strategies**. The Malaysian ESL TECW study frames collaborative writing as a non-linear, interactive process and emphasizes the need to scaffold students’ learning and align instruction with writing pedagogy [N1-F1]. The higher-education systematic review explicitly categorizes technologies across three writing phases—**prewriting, in-writing, and post-writing**—and maps six core instructional strategies across those phases [N3-F2]. These strategies include prewriting activities, scaffolding, peer review and feedback, collaborative revising and editing, reflective tasks, and collaborative note-taking [N3-F2].

The practices most commonly associated with technology use are those that require **shared authorship, structured pedagogical support, and task orchestration**. The review notes that frequently used platforms such as Google Docs, Moodle, Zoom, and WhatsApp function either as interactive collaborative spaces or as task-supporting tools for drafting, feedback, and revision [N3-F2]. This suggests that technology is especially salient for **collaborative idea construction, communication, and revision support**. The Malaysian study also emphasizes that teachers need strategies to elevate instruction aspects and guide context-specific guidelines for TECW procedures [N1-F1], reinforcing that technology is not merely a tool but a means to shape pedagogy.

Classification differs across studies and contexts because the framing varies by educational level and the nature of the writing task. The Malaysian study is centered on **ESL classrooms** and uses the UTAUT 2 model to examine challenges and strategies, focusing on implementation from cognitive, metacognitive, behavioural, and motivational aspects [N1-R2]. The higher-education systematic review, by contrast, is broader and methodologically more formal, analyzing empirical studies across 27 peer-reviewed sources and emphasizing intentional orchestration of technologies and instructional designs aligned with pedagogical goals [N3-F2]. It also explicitly categorizes technologies into five groups: collaborative study tools, classroom-based technologies, cloud-based word processors and shared documents, network-based social computing, and supporting tools [N3-F2]. This shows that the classification can be **context-sensitive**, with more explicit distinctions in higher education settings than in ESL teacher practice studies.

Overall, teacher practices are classified around **phase-based support, instructional strategy, and technology orchestration**. The most technology-associated practices are **collaborative drafting, feedback, revision, and task support** [N3-F2], while the classification itself varies by whether the focus is on ESL implementation, higher education, or general classroom practice [N1-F1][N3-F2].
